standard.title: Sample Size and Variation
standard.description: compare variations in distributions and proportions obtained from random samples of the same size drawn from a population and recognise the effect of sample size on this variation
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe distributions using summary statistics and displays (from AC9M7ST01, AC9M7ST02). Students understand sampling methods (from AC9M8ST02).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students compare distributions from multiple samples, recognise natural sampling variation, and understand that larger samples reduce variation.

nodes.label: Sampling variation — same population, different samples
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students recognise that samples from the same population produce different distributions due to chance, and describe the range of variation.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare two samples from the same population and explain why the distributions differ.
nodes.typical_width: Compare multiple samples using digital simulation; describe the variation in means, medians, and proportions across samples; connect to the concept of natural sampling variation.
wider: Investigate First Nations Ranger Groups' use of sampling to track species biodiversity — explain why they use sampling rather than census and how variation affects their conclusions.
Explore how data-driven decision-making uses distributions from multiple samples to identify reliable trends vs noise.

response_modes.reason: Sampling variation is a counter-intuitive concept — students expect samples from the same population to be identical. Multiple simulation contexts build the understanding that variation is expected and natural.

nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to investigate how variation changes as sample size increases — students who believe samples from the same population should be identical will misinterpret the Node 2 investigation, concluding that variation means something is wrong rather than recognising it as the expected phenomenon being studied.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations Ranger biodiversity monitoring offers advancing students a rich applied ecological context — the connection between statistical sampling variation and real conservation decision-making is significant and within Year 8 scope.
success_criteria: Explains that samples from the same population will naturally vary.
Describes the range of variation observed across multiple samples.
Does not conclude that sampling variation means the data is wrong.

nodes.label: Effect of sample size on variation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students investigate and describe how increasing sample size reduces variation in sample statistics, and apply this to making inferences.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare the variation in proportions from small vs large samples from the same population; state which varies less.
nodes.typical_width: Use digital simulations to investigate how variation changes as sample size increases; describe the pattern; apply to weather forecasting or other prediction contexts.
wider: Investigate the effect of adding or removing data on measures of central tendency and spread — connect to understanding of sample size sensitivity.
Explore how AI and machine learning systems require large training datasets to reduce variation in model performance — connect to the statistical principle.

response_modes.reason: The sample size-variation relationship requires students to systematically vary sample size, observe the pattern, and reason about why larger samples reduce variation. An explicit investigation scaffold prevents students drawing conclusions from one or two cases.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The connection between sample size and AI training data volume is a rich and contemporary extension — advancing students who make this connection are engaging with a significant real-world application of the statistical principle.
success_criteria: States that larger samples produce less variation in statistics.
Demonstrates the relationship using simulation data.
Applies the principle to justify a recommendation about sample size in a practical context.
